transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I suppose the honest answer is I’m here because I’ve been having thoughts I can’t seem to get away from. I keep thinking my wife and the kids would be better off if I just didn’t wake up one morning. It’s not just a passing thing anymore, it sits with me.

And lately I’ve been saying things like… I don’t need to see another winter. I know how that sounds. I don’t say it to be dramatic. It just feels like I’m worn out in a way I can’t explain very well, and that’s what brought me in.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the time, nearly every day, since these thoughts started?

I… I don’t know exactly how to answer that. “Most of the time, nearly every day” sounds very precise, and I haven’t really been keeping track of it that way.

I know I haven’t felt like myself, and I know those thoughts have been hanging around more than I’m comfortable with. But if you’re asking whether I wake up every single day and say, “I’m depressed,” I’m not sure. Some days it feels more like being tired all the way through, if that makes sense. Other times I just sort of sit there and don’t know what I’m feeling.

So… I guess I can’t give you a clean yes or no. I’ve felt low, yes, but I’m not sure how often counts as “nearly every day.”
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things the way you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you once liked?

Yes… yes, I have. That might be one of the clearest things, actually.

I used to have things in the week that I looked forward to. Bridge, for one. I wasn’t some professional card player or anything, but I liked the routine of it, seeing the same people, keeping my mind busy. And the garden… I used to fuss over that garden more than I probably needed to. I’d notice every little thing coming up, what needed trimming, what was blooming early. It gave me something to do with my hands.

Church cooking too — helping out in the kitchen, making food for people, being part of things. And Cubs games… even when they were breaking your heart, I still liked going or watching, talking about the game after.

Now I just… sit in my chair. I think about those things like they belong to somebody else. People will say, “Why don’t you come play bridge?” or “The garden needs attention,” and I know they’re right, but I can’t make myself care. It’s not that I decided I don’t like them anymore. It’s more like the part of me that used to feel anything about them has gone quiet.
Would you say that most days, your mood is clearly depressed, like a heaviness or sadness that doesn’t go away, even if it’s not intense?

I’m not sure I can say it as cleanly as that. “Clearly depressed” is where I get stuck, because I don’t always experience it as sadness exactly. It isn’t always like I’m crying or thinking, “I feel sad.” Sometimes it’s more like… a weight, yes, but other times it’s just this dullness, like everything has had the color taken out of it.

Most days, I know I’m not right. I know that much. I’ll sit there and the hours go by, and I don’t feel normal, but if you asked me to point to the feeling and name it, I’d have trouble. Some days it’s heavy. Some days it’s empty. Some days it’s just being tired of being myself, if that makes any sense.

So… maybe what you’re describing is close, but I don’t want to pretend I’m certain. I haven’t been measuring it day by day. I just know it’s been there a lot, and it doesn’t lift the way I keep hoping it will.
Would you say that most days, for most of the day, your mood has been clearly low or depressed, even if it’s not intensely sad?

I don’t know if I can say it that neatly. I know you’re trying to get at whether it’s there most of the day, most days, and I keep turning that over in my head like there ought to be a clear answer, but I haven’t really been keeping score.

There are long stretches where I feel low, or flat, or just not myself. But “clearly depressed” is hard for me, because sometimes it isn’t sadness in the usual way. It’s not always crying or feeling grief. Sometimes it’s more like I’m sitting there and everything feels far away, and I realize later that half the day has gone by and I’ve barely done anything.

So… I suppose it has been there a lot. More than I want to admit, probably. But if you’re asking me to say yes, definitely, most days for most of the day, I’m not sure I can be that exact. I just know I don’t feel right much of the time.
Have you felt a lack of energy or noticed that even small tasks feel exhausting, most days?

I don’t know that I can answer that very well. I mean… I’m old, so I don’t always know what’s age and what’s something else, if that makes sense.

There are days when I don’t do much, but I’m not sure I’d describe it as “exhausted” exactly. Sometimes I just sit there and don’t get started. Like I’ll look at something that ought to be done, something small, and I know it’s there, but I don’t quite move toward it. Whether that’s lack of energy or just… I don’t know, not having the push, I can’t really separate it.

I wouldn’t want to say most days for sure. I haven’t been paying attention in that way. I know I’m not as active as I used to be, but at 80 I suppose that can happen, and I don’t want to blame everything on one thing if I’m not certain. So… maybe a little, but I can’t give you a clean yes.
Have you found that you no longer take pleasure in almost anything, including things you used to enjoy?

Yes… I think that one I can answer more plainly. I don’t really take pleasure in much of anything now.

I used to have things, you know? Not grand things, but things that made the week feel like it had some shape to it. I used to look forward to bridge. I wasn’t even the best player at the table, but I liked the routine of it, seeing people, paying attention to the cards, the little jokes. And the garden — I used to fuss over that more than I probably needed to. I’d notice what was coming up, what needed trimming, what might bloom next. It mattered to me.

Church cooking, too. I used to like being part of that, feeling useful, even if it was just chopping or stirring or helping set things out. And Cubs games… I mean, I used to get a real lift out of going, or even just thinking about going.

Now I mostly just sit in my chair. That sounds pathetic when I say it, but it’s true. I can think about those things and I know, in my head, that I used to enjoy them. But I can’t seem to make myself care. It’s like the part of me that reached toward things has gone quiet. People will suggest something and I’ll say maybe, or I’ll think I should go, but there’s nothing pulling me there anymore.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?

Yes… yes, I’ve noticed that, and it bothers me quite a bit.

It’s not just forgetting a name here or there, the way people joke about at my age. It feels more like my mind won’t hold onto things long enough for me to use them. I help with some of the senior center budgets, or I used to be able to, and lately I can’t keep the numbers straight. I’ll look at a column and think I understand it, and then a minute later I don’t know what I just added or why it doesn’t make sense. I go back over the same figures again and again, and they don’t stay put in my head.

And it happens with ordinary things too. I’ll sit down with a bill, or I’ll open the calendar, and I’ll just stare at it. Not for a minute — sometimes it feels like half an hour goes by — and I still don’t know what I’m supposed to do next. Pay it? Write it down? Call someone? I can see the words, I can see the dates, but they don’t seem to turn into a decision.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I used to be fairly capable with that sort of thing. Not brilliant, but organized enough. Now I get stuck on things that ought to be simple, and the more I stare at them, the more tangled they get.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately—like eating much less or much more than usual, or losing or gaining weight without trying?

I’m not really sure. I haven’t been keeping track of my weight in any careful way, and I don’t weigh myself much unless someone at a doctor’s office does it.

As for appetite… I don’t know. Some days I eat because it’s mealtime more than because I feel hungry, but I can’t say for certain that it’s a real change. At my age meals get a bit irregular anyway, especially if I’m just fixing something for myself. I might have toast or soup or whatever is easiest, but I don’t know that that means I’m eating much less. And I don’t think I’ve noticed my clothes fitting very differently or anything like that.

So I suppose the honest answer is I haven’t really noticed a clear weight change, and I’m not sure about the appetite part. It hasn’t stood out to me the way some other things have.
Have you noticed that your thoughts have been moving more slowly than usual, or that you're moving more slowly—like everything takes more effort or just feels slowed down?

Yes… yes, that’s been happening. My wife notices it more than I do sometimes, or at least she says it out loud. She’ll tell me I’m moving like I’m walking through deep snow, and that’s actually what it feels like. Not painful exactly, but like every movement has resistance to it.

Getting dressed can take me a ridiculous amount of time. I’ll sit on the edge of the bed with a shirt in my hands and just… sit there. Then I’ll put one arm through, and it feels like I have to gather myself before doing the other. It’s not that I don’t know how to dress myself. It’s just so slow, and everything takes so much out of me.

Even crossing the kitchen feels like a project. I’ll think, “I should get a glass of water,” and then the distance from the chair to the sink seems much farther than it is. I get moving, but it’s like I’m dragging myself through something heavy. By the time I’m halfway into whatever I meant to do, I sometimes give up. I’ll just sit back down before I’ve really done much of anything.

It’s embarrassing. I know I must look slow. I can feel it in my body, and in my thoughts too, like there’s a delay between deciding to do something and actually doing it.
Have you completely stopped doing any of the activities you used to enjoy, even things that used to be meaningful or important to you?

Yes… I think I have, really. I don’t like saying it that plainly, but yes.

I used to have things I looked forward to. Bridge, for one — I used to enjoy the routine of it, seeing the same people, thinking through the hands, all of that. And the garden… I could spend a whole morning fussing over tomato plants or pulling weeds and feel like I’d done something good. Church cooking too — helping with meals, casseroles, whatever needed doing. It made me feel useful. And Cubs games… even when they were terrible, I still cared. I’d watch, or I’d go if someone asked, and I’d get worked up like it mattered.

Now it’s like none of it reaches me. People will mention bridge and I think, “I should go,” but I just sit there in my chair. The garden could probably use attention, and I know that, but I don’t feel pulled toward it. Church things come up, and instead of wanting to help, I just feel… blank. Even the Cubs, which sounds silly maybe, but that used to be one of those little pleasures. Now I can have the game on and not really watch it, or I don’t turn it on at all.

It isn’t that I decided I don’t like those things anymore. It’s more like I can’t make myself care. I sit in my chair and think about doing them, or I remember that I used to enjoy them, but there’s no spark there. Nothing catches.
Have you ever felt this way before, with a low mood and loss of interest in things, lasting for at least a couple of weeks or more?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I’ve had sad periods in my life, of course. At my age you don’t get to eighty without having losses and disappointments and spells where you’re not yourself for a while. There have been times I was down, or quieter, or not as eager to go out.

But whether it was like this, and whether it lasted at least a couple of weeks in the way you mean… I honestly don’t know. I don’t want to say yes if I’m just remembering ordinary hard times and dressing them up as something more. And I don’t want to say no either, because memory is a funny thing, and when you’re in the middle of feeling this low it can make the past look different.

I suppose what I can say is I don’t clearly remember another time that stands out to me the way this does. Not with the same feeling of things losing their color, if that makes sense. But as for whether I’ve “ever” had it before for two weeks or more… I’m just not certain.

It isn’t that I decided I don’t like those things anymore. It’s more like I can’t make myself care. I sit in my chair and think about doing them, or I remember that I used to enjoy them, but there’s no spark there. Nothing catches.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had a previous episode of depression that lasted at least two weeks, to establish whether this is a recurrent episode (F33.2) rather than a single episode (F32.2).
doctor.question: Have you ever felt this way before, with a low mood and loss of interest in things, lasting for at least a couple of weeks or more?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether there were prior episodes of low mood and loss of interest lasting at least a couple of weeks, but the provided symptom profile only covers the current episode and does not specify any past depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I’ve had sad periods in my life, of course. At my age you don’t get to eighty without having losses and disappointments and spells where you’re not yourself for a while. There have been times I was down, or quieter, or not as eager to go out.

But whether it was like this, and whether it lasted at least a couple of weeks in the way you mean… I honestly don’t know. I don’t want to say yes if I’m just remembering ordinary hard times and dressing them up as something more. And I don’t want to say no either, because memory is a funny thing, and when you’re in the middle of feeling this low it can make the past look different.

I suppose what I can say is I don’t clearly remember another time that stands out to me the way this does. Not with the same feeling of things losing their color, if that makes sense. But as for whether I’ve “ever” had it before for two weeks or more… I’m just not certain.
